covalent.note: Covalent radius; PubChem's values are those of Cordero et al., Dalton Trans. 2008, 2832. Value for l.s.; also 161(8)[h.s.].

vdw.note: Van der Waals radius (Los Alamos National Laboratory).

electronAffinity.note: PubChem lists no electron affinity for this element.

allen.note: Configuration energy (Allen electronegativity) in eV, not converted to the Pauling-like scale; Mann 2000b.

polarizability.note: Recommended value of the 2018 table: from experiment where it is precise enough, otherwise from high-level calculation.

crust.note: Jefferson Lab estimate for Earth's crust, via PubChem ('9.50×10² milligrams per kilogram').

ocean.note: Jefferson Lab estimate for sea water, via PubChem ('2×10⁻⁴ milligrams per liter').

solar.note: Proto-solar (4.567 Ga ago) elemental mass fraction, column 'Elemental Mass Fractions' of ESM Table A13; the table gives no uncertainty (relative sigma of N(E) in Table 6 applies).

solarLogEps.note: A(E) = log10(N_E/N_H) + 12, 'Solar System Present' log (E/H)+12; basis: average of solar and meteoritic values. The table prints +-0.00 dex (i.e. below 0.005 dex); unc omitted so that no zero uncertainty is displayed.

body.note: In a 70 kg reference adult (ICRP Publication 23, 1975, Table 110).

crystal.structure: cubic, α-Mn type (complex body-centred cubic cell)
crystal.reference: Gazzara, C. P.; Middleton, R. M.; Weiss, R. J.; Hall, E. O. (1967). Acta Crystallographica 22, 859.
crystal.note: α-Mn has 58 atoms per conventional cell on four independent sites. Measured at 298 K.

tonnesPerYear.note: World mine production, manganese content, 2025 (USGS: 20,000 thousand metric tons).

unitValue.note: Price, average, manganese content, cost, insurance, and freight, China, dollars per metric ton unit [Manganese], 2025; per kg of the material named, as USGS gives it.

molarHeatCapacity.note: At 25 °C and 1 bar, per mole of atoms, for the form stable at 25 °C (CRC Handbook, 95th ed.).

uses.text: Mainly used in making iron and steel, as ferromanganese and silicomanganese.
Smaller uses: animal feed, fertilisers and brick colourant.

sectors.text: Manganese is part of the cathodes of nickel-manganese-cobalt (NMC) batteries and of the steel in wind turbines.
Manganese goes into vehicle batteries, fuel cells, industrial heat pumps and hydrogen-based steelmaking, according to the JRC's study of strategic technologies.
Manganese goes into the networks that carry data, data centres (storage and servers) and phones, tablets and laptops, according to the JRC's study of strategic technologies.

allotropes.name: α-manganese
allotropes.note: A complicated cubic structure with 58 atoms per cell: hard and brittle.

allotropes.name: β-, γ- and δ-manganese
allotropes.note: On heating, a second complex cubic form (20 atoms per cell), then face-centred and body-centred cubic forms.

hazardStatements.text: Toxic to aquatic life with long lasting effects
Harmful to aquatic life with long lasting effects

hazards.note: Aggregated by PubChem from 3101 reports by companies to the ECHA C&L Inventory; the percentage after a statement is the share of reports that give it. 46.1 % of the reports (1429 of 3101) say manganese does not meet the GHS hazard criteria.

crust.note: Earth's crust, as given (mg/kg is parts per million by mass).

ocean.note: Sea water, mg/L read as mg/kg: a litre of sea water is taken as one kilogram (it is slightly heavier; the difference cannot be seen on a logarithmic scale).

body.note: Grams in the 70 kg reference adult of ICRP Publication 23, divided by its mass.

origin.note: Read off Fig. 39 at the dotted 'age of the Sun' line (t = 9.2 Gyr after the Big Bang, 4.6 Gyr ago): pixel fractions of the stacked areas (agb 0.080, massive_stars 0.151, white_dwarfs 0.768); quantised to 0.05. Stack height 63 px. Paper: 'For the elements from Ne to Ge, the newly synthesized amounts are very small for AGB stars, and the small green areas are mostly for mass loss.'

air.text: Oxidises superficially in air; burns with a bright light when heated.

water.text: Decomposes water slowly in the cold and quickly when heated, giving hydrogen.

acids.text: Dissolves in dilute mineral acids with hydrogen given off, forming manganese(II) salts.

splitting.note: 3d5 4s2 a6S5/2 ground level, Davis, Wright and Balling (1971). A is converted from -2.416e-3 cm-1 in arXiv:2211.12797 Table 1 (1 cm-1 = 29979.2458 MHz). That document gives no uncertainty, so A_unc is only the rounding of the tabulated digits and limits the splitting. The B magnitude and uncertainty come from arXiv:1508.06207, which prints it as positive. The sign follows arXiv:2211.12797 (negative). Changing the sign moves the width by only 0.017 MHz, which is included in unc_Hz. Splitting = width of the ground-level hyperfine manifold (F = 0 to 5), from A and B.

plantRole.text: Four manganese atoms and one calcium atom form the cluster in photosystem II that splits water and releases oxygen.

humanRole.text: Part of enzymes such as mitochondrial superoxide dismutase and arginase.

roles.text: Activates enzymes that build cartilage and bone; chicks short of it develop deformed legs (perosis).
In yeast it serves the mitochondrial superoxide dismutase and the sugar-transferring enzymes that decorate secreted proteins.
Many bacteria use it in enzymes; Deinococcus radiodurans even switches the way it breaks down glucose with the amount of manganese it holds.

uptake.text: Only as the divalent ion Mn²⁺

deficiency.text: The youngest leaves yellow faintly between the veins, because manganese hardly moves out of older leaves; severe shortage adds brown spots. In the field cereals show it as patchy 'light spot disease', and peas as 'marsh spot' in their seeds.
Oats, barley, wheat, soybean and peach are susceptible, rye is not. Manganese-short plants are also more easily killed by frost and more open to root-rot fungi such as take-all.

toxicity.text: Too much shows as small brown spots on mature leaves, and in soybean as crinkled leaves. Tolerance differs enormously: growth falls at about 200 mg per kg of shoot dry matter in maize but only at about 5,300 in sunflower.

soil.text: How much manganese is available swings with soil pH, moisture and air: limy, sandy and peaty soils tend to hold too little, while acid or waterlogged soils release too much.

partners.text: On acid tropical soils, manganese toxicity often holds back nitrogen fixation by legumes; liming helps, and mycorrhizal fungi ease the toxicity.
Plants with arbuscular mycorrhiza often take up less manganese than plants without the fungus, unlike zinc and copper, of which they take up more.

wild.text: Plants that tolerate a lot of manganese, such as sunflower and stinging nettle, store the excess in the cell walls at the base of their leaf hairs, which turn dark.

forest.text: Manganese rarely limits forests (perhaps on some limestone soils in New Zealand and South Africa), and manganese toxicity, which can harm farm crops, has not been reported in forests.

levels.note: Table 2.20. Low: 10–20; high: 200–250; the excess class is printed as '350' (the '>' seems lost in the scan).

levels.part: leaves from the base of new shoots

levels.note: Possible deficiency below this level (Carter 1992, cited in chapter 13); the book says micronutrient critical levels in trees are not well established.

history.nameOrigin: From manganesia, a medieval variant of magnesia, the old name shared by its black oxide ore (pyrolusite).
history.note: Scheele recognized a new metal in pyrolusite and Gahn reduced the oxide to the metal the same year; the map dot marks Scheele's Uppsala. CIAAW instead links the name to the Latin magnes, 'magnet'.

prose.text: Manganese is a hard, brittle, grey transition metal; most of it goes into steel, which it toughens, and it also forms the dark manganese dioxide inside ordinary alkaline batteries. Life uses it in a remarkable place: in photosystem II of plants and algae, a cluster of four manganese atoms and one calcium atom pulls electrons from water, and almost all the oxygen in the air was released there. The atom has a half-filled 3d subshell, [Ar] 3d⁵ 4s², with five unpaired electrons whose spins all point the same way; their orbital motions cancel, giving an S-type ground term, ⁶S₅/₂.
